questions.question: When are events $A$ and $B$ conditionally independent given $C$?
options: When $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ holds, without conditioning
When $P(A\cap B\mid C)=P(A\mid C)P(B\mid C)$
When $A\cap B=\varnothing$
When $P(C)=0$

questions.question: What condition is required for conditioning on $C$?
options: $C=\varnothing$
$C=A\cup B$ always

questions.question: What does conditional independence mean intuitively?
options: Two events cannot both occur once certain information is known
Two events stop influencing each other once some information is known
Two events independent overall stay independent after any conditioning
Two events are independent before any information is known

questions.question: If $P(A\mid C)=0.4$, $P(B\mid C)=0.5$, and $A,B$ are conditionally independent given $C$, what is $P(A\cap B\mid C)$?
If $P(A\cap B\mid C)=0.12$, $P(A\mid C)=0.3$, and $P(B\mid C)=0.4$, are $A$ and $B$ conditionally independent given $C$?
options: No, because all conditional probabilities differ
Yes, because $P(C)=0$
Yes, because $0.3\cdot0.4=0.12$
No, because conditional independence is disjointness

questions.question: Why can marginal dependence coexist with conditional independence?
options: Conditioning on any event removes the dependence between two events
Dependence is checked given $C$, conditional independence overall
Events with a common cause are independent until we condition on it
A common cause creates association that disappears given the cause

questions.question: A hospital records two symptoms. They are associated overall, but after conditioning on disease status the association disappears. What is the best description?
options: The symptoms are disjoint, meaning they cannot occur together at all
The symptoms are independent overall but dependent given disease status
The symptoms are conditionally independent given disease status
One symptom directly causes the other, whatever the disease status

questions.question: Let $A,B,C$ be events with $\mathbb{P}(A\cap C)>0$. Which equality is equivalent to conditional independence of $A$ and $B$ given $C$?
options: $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A\cap C)=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)$
$\mathbb{P}(B\mid A\cap C)=\mathbb{P}(B)$
$\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)=\mathbb{P}(B)$
$\mathbb{P}(B\mid A\cap C)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)$

questions.question: A fair coin or a coin with heads probability $0.9$ is chosen, each with probability $\tfrac12$, and tossed twice. Given the chosen coin, the two tosses are independent. Let $H_1$, $H_2$ be heads on the first and second toss. Which statement is correct?
options: $\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2)=0.53\ne\mathbb{P}(H_1)\mathbb{P}(H_2)$, so $H_1,H_2$ are dependent
$\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2)=0.49=\mathbb{P}(H_1)\mathbb{P}(H_2)$, so $H_1,H_2$ are independent
$\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2)=0.53$, but $H_1,H_2$ are independent since they are given the coin
$\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2)=0.7$, so $H_1,H_2$ are dependent

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed independently. Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the events of heads on the first and on the second toss, and let $C$ be the event that at least one of the two tosses shows heads. Which statement about $H_1$ and $H_2$ given $C$ is correct?
options: They are conditionally independent given $C$, because independence of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is kept under conditioning on any $C$ with $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$.
They are conditionally independent given $C$, because $\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2\mid C)=\frac{1}{4}=\mathbb{P}(H_1)\mathbb{P}(H_2)$.
They are not conditionally independent given $C$, because $\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2\mid C)=\frac{1}{3}$ but $\mathbb{P}(H_1\mid C)\mathbb{P}(H_2\mid C)=\frac{4}{9}$.
They are conditionally independent given $C$, because $H_1\subseteq C$ and $H_2\subseteq C$, so conditioning on $C$ only rescales and keeps the factorization.
